newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE-Designer fuses modernity and Asian philosophy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Designer fuses modernity and Asian philosophy.

text.p: As a child, Alan Chan made pinball machines with rubber bands and old fruit crates, never dreaming he would grow up to become one of Asia's most sought-after designers.
His cramped office in Hong Kong's Wanchai entertainment district is stuffed with glass clocks, tasteful ceramics and elegant boxes, all conceived by Chan.
The office evinces a frenzied creativity and exudes Chan's stamp: a fusion of traditional Chinese philosophy and modern design.

Looking serious in round glasses, Chan says that in the cut-throat competition of the Pacific century -- and he firmly believes the future is in Asia -- strong design helps move goods off supermarket shelves into consumers' homes.
He also has a personal cultural mission: dusting off ancient philosophies for fresh design uses, which he believes actually helps stimulate the interest of Asians in their own culture.
Dozens of design awards stacked in disorderly piles against the office walls show clearly that others agree.
MELDING EAST AND WEST
The wiry, goateed Chan says his distinctive style is at its core a marriage of east and west.

In a poster created for a 1991 exhibition in Tokyo, Chan traced with a finger the Chinese word for "east" on grainy sand illuminated by a ray of sunlight. Turning the image upside down reveals English letters forming the word "west".
His plays on ideas that draw on familiar Asian motifs have struck a chord all over the Pacific basin, particularly in design-obsessed Japan.

His best-selling item is a gift box with four canisters of tea decorated with the calendar girls of the 1930s, ivory-skinned Chinese women with figure-hugging cheung-sams, priced at HK$168 (US$21.70).
"When I capitalise on the Chinese cultural elements and try to revitalise or reactivate the commercial world, I always bear in mind I'm also playing the role of promoting a culture," Chan says.
In his native Hong Kong, Chan is a design guru. Throw a stone in the British colony's Central business district and you are likely to hit one of his designs, Chan himself says with pride.
His displays have mushroomed in key areas across the city, in prestige supermarkets and hotels such as the Regent and Marriott and upscale department store Seibu.
PRESERVING AN ASIAN IDENTITY

Seven years ago Chan started his own company with his wife, a secretary and one assistant. The business has exploded into a 40-person outfit and given birth to offshoots Alan Chan Design and Alan Chan Creations.
"We were nominated as one of the top ten design companies in the world by Graphis in New York," Chan says happily.
Chan's success lies in forging a smart new Asian identity that reflects both the region's spectacular economic development and its traditional values.
"We live in the comfort of all this technology, but at the same time, being Chinese, we do need to have this cultural input to keep an essence, an identity of being yourself," Chan says.
Almost 80 percent of Chan's work serves brand and corporate identity. The elegant "S"-shaped logo Chan conjured up for Seibu exemplifies his philosophy.
Chan was inspired by an antique jade carving of a pair of carp curved snugly around each other, their tails flipping in opposite directions.
In Chinese, the word for "fish" sounds the same as the word for "abundance", explains Chan.

"To feature the graphic on the bags and all the rest of the material, I have arranged the logo in a continuously cyclical manner, because the growth of prosperity is also philosphically important to the Chinese and Asians," he says.
THE FUTURE OF DESIGN IS IN ASIA
In Southeast Asia, the generation of Filipinos, Indonesians, Thais and Malaysians who went abroad to study have streamed home as their country's economies have expanded, Chan says.
They have taken the reins of their parents' businesses and made them more international and cosmopolitan, Chan says.
In search of a new image, they are keen to tap design resources from their own Asian heritages.
"There is a lot of wisdom and knowledge given by our ancestors which I think is still applicable to our everyday life," Chan says.
Chan has undertaken projects in Malaysia's downtown Kuala Lumpur and in Thailand and is waiting for China to throw open its doors to design concepts.
"There is a big demand for brand and corporate identity system in China that will revitalise their state sector.
"I'm predicting that within the next five to ten years, the whole face of Asia will be born again," he says.
